title: How To Manage Large Class Sizes
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that large class sizes don't inherently cause behavior problems—they simply amplify whatever classroom management deficiencies already exist. With small classes, mistakes are more forgiving; with large ones, sloppy routines, weak relationships, and inconsistency compound quickly into real trouble. He insists his site's strategies are designed to work at any class size, since teachers should never recommend something that only functions with fewer students. The piece reassures teachers that the same fulfilling, well-behaved classroom is achievable regardless of roster size, provided the fundamentals are solid.
points: Large class sizes don't create behavior problems on their own; they amplify existing weaknesses in a teacher's classroom management.
Mistakes that are easily absorbed in a small class can multiply into significant misbehavior as class size grows.
Strategies are only genuinely effective if they work regardless of class size—an explicit design principle behind the site's advice.
As class size increases, teachers need sharper consistency and stronger relationship-building despite less individual time per student.
The same well-behaved, fulfilling classroom is achievable at six students or sixty, given the right approach.
quotes: With a class of sixteen to twenty students you can afford to cut corners. You can make big mistakes and not lose control of your classroom.
You see, when class sizes reach upwards of twenty students, stretching to near forty and forty-five in some cases, there is less room for error.
Here at Smart Classroom Management our approach is the same regardless of how many students you have in your class.

This is why so many teachers struggle as class sizes escalate. Behavior worsens not so much because of the increase in students, but because the teacher doesn’t have the classroom management skills to deal with it.
You can have the well-behaved class you want no matter the size.
